It began after a fatty meal. No position has relieved it. Taking a deep breath and eating worsen it. I tried an antacid without relief. I had two shorter episodes after meals last month. I feel nauseated. I vomited twice. I felt feverish this morning.

Patient perspective: Will I have to have surgery?

PMH: No known gallstones or chronic disease.

PSH: Cesarean delivery 5 years ago.

Meds: No daily medicines; one dose of antacid last night.

Allergies: Codeine causes severe nausea, without rash or breathing problems.

SH: Never smoked tobacco. One glass of wine monthly. No recreational drugs. Office manager; lives with husband and child; last period 2 weeks ago, no pregnancy suspected.

FH: My mother is fifty-four and she had gallbladder surgery.; My father is fifty-six and he has diabetes.; My brother is thirty-one and he's healthy.

ROS: Gastrointestinal - Reports nausea. Reports vomiting. Denies jaundice. General - Reports fever. Denies chills. Denies weight loss. Urinary - Denies dysuria. Denies hematuria. Denies frequency.
model_note.O:
Vitals: T 100.8 F oral, P 100 bpm, BP 128/78 mmHg, R 18 rpm, Pulse Ox 98% on room air, Ht 5' 7", Wt 165 lbs

General: Alert and uncomfortable, holding right upper abdomen.

Heart: Regular rhythm without murmur.

Lungs: Clear breath sounds at both posterior bases.

Abd: Abdomen not distended; healed lower abdominal scar. Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants. Right upper quadrant tenderness. Inspiratory arrest with right subcostal palpation during Murphy maneuver. Tympanitic away from the liver region.

HEENT: Conjunctivae pink and sclerae not icteric.

Osteopathic: T5 paraspinal tissue texture change with mild tenderness on the right.

Skin: No visible rash on the inspected arms.
P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department today for surgical evaluation of persistent pain and fever; obtain right upper quadrant ultrasound, CBC, liver tests, bilirubin and lipase; provide clinician-directed fluids and analgesia and consider antibiotics; explain why persistent pain differs from a brief uncomplicated biliary episode.

2. Obtain ECG and appropriate cardiac biomarkers if ischemia remains plausible; reassess cardiopulmonary symptoms and risk factors; explain that upper abdominal discomfort can occasionally come from the heart; consult the emergency/cardiology team for concerning findings.

3. After urgent biliary and cardiac causes are assessed, consider H. pylori testing and directed acid suppression if the persistent pattern supports peptic disease; coordinate testing before acid suppression or with the appropriate PPI washout. Review ulcer/NSAID history and explain prompt reassessment for black stools, vomiting blood or abrupt severe pain.

cc: Persistent right upper abdominal pain after eating

HPI: 28 yo f. Patient reports: It began 10 hours ago. It is under the right ribs. It travels toward my right shoulder blade. It is a steady deep ache. It is 8/10. It has stayed constant for hours. It began after a fatty meal. No position has relieved it. Taking a deep breath and eating worsen it. I tried an antacid without relief. I had two shorter episodes after meals last month. I feel nauseated. I vomited twice. I felt feverish this morning.

Patient perspective: Will I have to have surgery?

Abd: Abdomen not distended; healed lower abdominal scar. Bowel sounds present in all four quadrants. Right upper quadrant tenderness. Inspiratory arrest with right subcostal palpation during Murphy maneuver. Tympanitic away from the liver region.

HEENT: Conjunctivae pink and sclerae not icteric.

P: 1. Transfer to the emergency department today for surgical evaluation of persistent pain and fever; obtain right upper quadrant ultrasound, CBC, liver tests, bilirubin and lipase; provide clinician-directed fluids and analgesia and consider antibiotics; explain why persistent pain differs from a brief uncomplicated biliary episode. Explain ultrasound in plain language and check the patient’s understanding before discussing the next steps.

2. Obtain ECG and appropriate cardiac biomarkers if ischemia remains plausible; reassess cardiopulmonary symptoms and risk factors; explain that upper abdominal discomfort can occasionally come from the heart; consult the emergency/cardiology team for concerning findings.

3. After urgent biliary and cardiac causes are assessed, consider H. pylori testing and directed acid suppression if the persistent pattern supports peptic disease; coordinate testing before acid suppression or with the appropriate PPI washout. Review ulcer/NSAID history and explain prompt reassessment for black stools, vomiting blood or abrupt severe pain.
